item.title: Should the Crowd Program the Car?
item.description: A playful, dramatized interview with fictional correspondent Dr. Rowan Field on crowdsourced moral preferences for autonomous vehicles, and why a preference distribution is not a decision procedure.

item.title: Building the Decider
item.description: A playful, dramatized interview with fictional correspondent Dr. Rowan Field on what it takes to turn crowdsourced moral preferences into a machine that actually decides: a utility model fit to human judgements, a voting rule that aggregates them, and the gap between an aggregate that can be computed and one that can only be estimated.

item.title: Who Gets Blamed When Both Are Wrong
item.description: A playful, dramatized interview with fictional correspondent Dr. Rowan Field on who the public blames when a human driver and an automated system both make mistakes — and why that blame pattern may quietly weaken the liability pressure meant to force safer designs.
item.content:encoded:
Produced: Thu, 05 Nov 2026 10:33:24 +0000

This is a synthetic/dramatized interview with fictional research correspondent Dr. Rowan Field. Rowan is a fictional composite; no cited author was interviewed or is speaking through Rowan. Dialogue paraphrases and synthesizes the research, preserves evidence limits, and contains no fabricated author quotations.

This is an AI-generated summary that may contain errors and is not a substitute for reading the cited sources.

Full source notes, evidence limitations, and direct Zotero links

  1. Edmond Awad, Sydney Levine, Max Kleiman-Weiner, Sohan Dsouza, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Azim Shariff, Jean-François Bonnefon, and Iyad Rahwan. "Drivers are blamed more than their automated cars when both make mistakes." *Nature Human Behaviour* 4, 2020, pp. 134–143 (published online 28 October 2019). [Zotero file](https://www.zotero.org/groups/2412036/items/EIUADNKU) · [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-019-0762-8)
  2. Berkeley J. Dietvorst, Joseph P. Simmons, and Cade Massey. "Algorithm aversion: people erroneously avoid algorithms after seeing them err." *Journal of Experimental Psychology: General* 144(1), 2015, pp. 114–126. Cited by Awad et al. as prior reason to expect machines to be judged more harshly after error.
  3. Bertram F. Malle, Matthias Scheutz, Thomas Arnold, John Voiklis, and Corey Cusimano. "Sacrifice one for the good of many? People apply different moral norms to human and robot agents." *Proceedings of the Tenth Annual ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction*, 2015, pp. 117–124. Cited as prior evidence of divergent moral norms for robot versus human agents.
  4. Ralph Nader. *Unsafe at Any Speed: The Designed-In Dangers of the American Automobile.* Grossman, 1965. The campaigning text behind the crashworthiness shift; the historical framing is the authors', and this episode attributes it to them rather than presenting it as their own finding.
  5. Ethics Commission on Automated and Connected Driving. *Report.* Federal Ministry of Transport and Digital Infrastructure (Germany), June 2017. Source of the prohibition on trading lives against each other, cited by Awad et al. in discussing why the dilemma framing may dissolve the notion of a "mistake."
